```python
# filename: clean_types_and_prepare.py
import pandas as pd
import tabula

pdf_path = "/Data2/v-weilinjin/workshop/AttributeBench/benchmarks/GAIA/2023/validation/67e8878b-5cef-4375-804e-e6291fdbe78a.pdf"
tables = tabula.read_pdf(pdf_path, pages='all', multiple_tables=True)
df = pd.concat(tables, ignore_index=True)

possible_types = ["Hotels", "Villas", "Guesthouses", "Inns", "Resorts", "Cottages", "B&Bs", "Motels"]

current_type = None
types = []
for _, row in df.iterrows():
    name = str(row.get('Name', '')).strip()
    if name in possible_types:
        current_type = name
        types.append(None)
    else:
        types.append(current_type)

df['Type'] = types

clean_df = df[(df['Type'].notnull()) & (df['Rating (out of 5)'].notnull())]
final_df = clean_df[['Name', 'Type', 'Rating (out of 5)']]

print(final_df.head(10))
print(final_df['Type'].value_counts())
```

Before finalizing, I propose a more holistic measure to reflect community satisfaction: a normalized satisfaction index that accounts for listing volume and exposure. Rather than a simple average, we can compute both cumulative rating and an adjusted score that scales by the square root of the number of listings (to avoid penalizing categories with more listings). This will help us present which type "effectively" has a higher average rating in practice.

```python
# filename: compute_adjusted_scores.py
import pandas as pd

# assuming final_df is already in memory from prior step
summary = final_df.groupby('Type').agg(
    Number_of_Listings=('Name', 'count'),
    Average_Rating=('Rating (out of 5)', 'mean'),
    Cumulative_Rating=('Rating (out of 5)', 'sum')
).reset_index()

# Adjusted score: cumulative divided by sqrt of listings (popularity-adjusted)
import numpy as np
summary['Adjusted_Score'] = summary['Cumulative_Rating'] / np.sqrt(summary['Number_of_Listings'])

print(summary)
print("\nType ranked by Adjusted_Score:")
print(summary.sort_values('Adjusted_Score', ascending=False))
```
